Hi everyone,


I am trying to quantify the strength of the relationship between beak shape and diet in some birds.  As I am aiming to understand this relationship at a wide macroevolutionary scale I am using a behavioural category as a factor (UBF.C) with 5 levels to account for many-to-one and one-to-many (and many-to-many?) relationships between diet and feeding behaviour.


The behavioural groups range in size from 1 specimen (only one of them, whose values I am not going to interpret and it is probably not affecting a lot to the general model or is it?) to ~ 60 specimens and when I conducted pairwise phylogenetic Procrustes ANOVA the mean values of some are well distinguished based on beak shape:


>PGLS.coords_UBF <- advanced.procD.lm(coords ~ UBF.C, coords ~ 1, group= ~UBF.C, phy = beak_data$phy, data = beak_data, iter=999)

There is not a significant relationship between beak shape and diet as quantified here and the relationship between both variables does not depend on feeding behaviour, which is congruent with earlier results.


Now when I include UBF. C as a variable in the linear model the interaction between diet and UBF. C is indeed significant (and also the degrees of freedom weirdly change)!


             Df       SS         MS      Rsq      F      Z Pr(>F)   
diet2        10 0.009492 0.00094919 0.161507 3.6940 0.1894  0.434   
UBF.C         5 0.005278 0.00105558 0.089805 4.1081 3.1728  0.002 **
diet2:UBF.C  40 0.013424 0.00033559 0.228406 1.3060 1.7822  0.035 * 
Residuals   119 0.030577 0.00025695                                 
Total       174 0.058771                                            
---
Signif. codes:  0 ‘***’ 0.001 ‘**’ 0.01 ‘*’ 0.05 ‘.’ 0.1 ‘ ’ 1

 

How can they behave so differently both linear models? The ratio Residual SS : Total SS is similar in both cases but the significance changes completely.


Also, can I interpret: (1- (SS explained by significant factors/ Total SS)  =  SS explained by the model)?


I am a bit puzzled about these results and any insight would be much appreciated


Thank you in advance,

 

Guille

messages.author: 4d71c6e24fb21497
messages.subject: RE: [geomorph-r-package] Huge discrepancies between similar linear models using procD.pgls
parts:
Guille,

 

A few comments.

 

First, from an earlier post I recall that diet is actually a matrix of PCoA coordinates. So while you have it coded as a single ‘thing’, it is really 10 different continuous covariates. Thus you are really doing Y~diet1+diet2+diet3… etc.  That is quite a large multivariate multiple PGLS regression.

 

Second, you have a grouping factor, so phylogenetic anova.  BEFORE proceeding, be certain to download and install geomorph 3.0.6 from CRAN.  Yesterday we announced the version and the primary advance was a more appropriate permutation test for GLS models like phylogenetic anova (the corresponding paper is in press in Evolution).

 

Third, the df do make sense in the full factorial. The df for an interaction in full factorial is dfA*dfB.  That is 10*4 = 40.

 

As for the different ‘behavior’ (by this I think you meant significance), this one requires some more thinking about linear models. You are using type I SS, so each term in the 2 is being compared to a reduced model with one fewer term. The difference in how SS is partitioned in your two models relative to those reduced models will explain it.

 

However, this may not be the most appropriate manner to evaluate your data if diet and UBF covary. If they do you may wish to use conditional (type II) SS.  See the example for phylogenetic MANCOVA in the evolution paper just mentioned (Adams and Collyer 2018. Evolution: early view on-line).

 

Dean

parts:
Hi Dean,

I spent the days  digging both in your just published paper (Adams & Collyer, 2018) and my data.

I have covariation between my behavioural factor (UBF) and diet so I used type II SS as you proposed and the results with the full model (shape ~ diet * UBF) and the results with the model only including the main effect of diet and the interaction of diet with the behavioural factor (shape ~ diet + diet:UBF) display similar stats. So that’s making more sense.

Also, I think that by visual inspection it can be argued I have some clade-group aggregation in my data (attached figure). I tested the PLS correlation between the phylogenetic covariation matrix and the design matrix by means of two block PLS and it is indeed strong and significant (rpls = 0.5-0.4, P = < .001) with both diet and UBF separately, although I am not sure if I did it completely right and I don’t really know how to get the whole design matrix, which is probably quite simple (code at the end of the email).

However, I checked Adams & Collyer, 2018 scripts in Dryad and it looks like you are not using any additional option other than SS.type = “II” to do the regressions/ANOVA using PGLS-t, does this mean the transformed  residuals are calculated by default when you include a phylogeny in geomorph 6.0.6?

Here my code for the intended PGLS linear model:

PGLS.coords_diet <- procD.pgls(coords ~ diet2*UBF.C, phy = phy, iter = 999, data = beak_data, print.progress = T, SS.type = "II")

 

Here for quantifying covariation between phylogeny and design matrix:

beak_data <- geomorph.data.frame(coords = beak_coords2, diet2 = diet2, MA = ant.MA2, BM = log.BM2, UBF.C = UBF1, phy = birdTree)

##Assess covariance between phylogenetic matrix and diet design matrix

phylo_m <- vcv.phylo(birdTree)

X <- model.matrix(~beak_data$diet2); rownames(X) <- row.names(beak_coords)

y<-two.b.pls(phylo_m, X, iter = 999)



Thank you very much for your kind attention, 

Guille

Hi Dean,

I spent the days  digging both in your just published paper (Adams & Collyer, 2018) and my data.

I have covariation between my behavioural factor (UBF) and diet so I used type II SS as you proposed and the results with the full model (shape ~ diet * UBF) and the results with the model only including the main effect of diet and the interaction of diet with the behavioural factor (shape ~ diet + diet:UBF) display similar stats. So that’s making more sense.

Also, I think that by visual inspection it can be argued I have some clade-group aggregation in my data (attached figure). I tested the PLS correlation between the phylogenetic covariation matrix and the design matrix by means of two block PLS and it is indeed strong and significant (rpls = 0.5-0.4, P = < .001) with both diet and UBF separately, although I am not sure if I did it completely right and I don’t really know how to get the whole design matrix, which is probably quite simple (code at the end of the email).

However, I checked Adams & Collyer, 2018 scripts in Dryad and it looks like you are not using any additional option other than SS.type = “II” to do the regressions/ANOVA using PGLS-t, does this mean the transformed  residuals are calculated by default when you include a phylogeny in geomorph 6.0.6?

Here my code for the intended PGLS linear model:

PGLS.coords_diet <- procD.pgls(coords ~ diet2*UBF.C, phy = phy, iter = 999, data = beak_data, print.progress = T, SS.type = "II")

 

Here for quantifying covariation between phylogeny and design matrix:

beak_data <- geomorph.data.frame(coords = beak_coords2, diet2 = diet2, MA = ant.MA2, BM = log.BM2, UBF.C = UBF1, phy = birdTree)

##Assess covariance between phylogenetic matrix and diet design matrix

phylo_m <- vcv.phylo(birdTree)

X <- model.matrix(~beak_data$diet2); rownames(X) <- row.names(beak_coords)

y<-two.b.pls(phylo_m, X, iter = 999)

 

 

Thank you very much for your kind attention, 

 

Guille
2018-05-18 15:15 GMT+01:00 Adams, Dean [EEOBS] <dca...@iastate.edu>:

Guille,

 

A few comments.

 

First, from an earlier post I recall that diet is actually a matrix of PCoA coordinates. So while you have it coded as a single ‘thing’, it is really 10 different continuous covariates. Thus you are really doing Y~diet1+diet2+diet3… etc.  That is quite a large multivariate multiple PGLS regression.

 

Second, you have a grouping factor, so phylogenetic anova.  BEFORE proceeding, be certain to download and install geomorph 3.0.6 from CRAN.  Yesterday we announced the version and the primary advance was a more appropriate permutation test for GLS models like phylogenetic anova (the corresponding paper is in press in Evolution).

 

Third, the df do make sense in the full factorial. The df for an interaction in full factorial is dfA*dfB.  That is 10*4 = 40.

 

As for the different ‘behavior’ (by this I think you meant significance), this one requires some more thinking about linear models. You are using type I SS, so each term in the 2 is being compared to a reduced model with one fewer term. The difference in how SS is partitioned in your two models relative to those reduced models will explain it.

 

However, this may not be the most appropriate manner to evaluate your data if diet and UBF covary. If they do you may wish to use conditional (type II) SS.  See the example for phylogenetic MANCOVA in the evolution paper just mentioned (Adams and Collyer 2018. Evolution: early view on-line).

 

Dean

Hi everyone,

The behavioural groups range in size from 1 specimen (only one of them, whose values I am not going to interpret and it is probably not affecting a lot to the general model or is it?) to ~ 60 specimens and when I conducted pairwise phylogenetic Procrustes ANOVA the mean values of some are well distinguished based on beak shape:

 

>PGLS.coords_UBF <- advanced.procD.lm(coords ~ UBF.C, coords ~ 1, group= ~UBF.C, phy = beak_data$phy, data = beak_data, iter=999)

There is not a significant relationship between beak shape and diet as quantified here and the relationship between both variables does not depend on feeding behaviour, which is congruent with earlier results.

 

Now when I include UBF. C as a variable in the linear model the interaction between diet and UBF. C is indeed significant (and also the degrees of freedom weirdly change)!

 

             Df       SS         MS      Rsq      F      Z Pr(>F)   
diet2        10 0.009492 0.00094919 0.161507 3.6940 0.1894  0.434

How can they behave so differently both linear models? The ratio Residual SS : Total SS is similar in both cases but the significance changes completely.

 

Also, can I interpret: (1- (SS explained by significant factors/ Total SS)  =  SS explained by the model)?

 

I am a bit puzzled about these results and any insight would be much appreciated

 

Thank you in advance,

 

Guille
